intro: Five modules follow the five Linux Essentials 2.0 topics and their weights. Each one has a study guide, exam tips, key terms, visual slides, and a narrated lesson. Practice the commands in the Labs tab, and use LPI's free official learning materials alongside these modules.

modules.title: The Linux operating system and open source software
modules.summary: Know what Linux is, how distributions differ, the major open source applications, how open source licenses work, and where Linux runs: desktops, servers, virtual machines, containers, the cloud, and WSL.

guide.html: Topic 011 is 7 of the 40 exam points. It's mostly conceptual: recognizing distributions, applications, licenses, and the places Linux is used. No commands to memorize here, but the vocabulary shows up throughout the exam.

Linux is a kernel, released by Linus Torvalds in 1991. A distribution combines the kernel with GNU tools, libraries, a package manager, an installer, and applications. Families matter because they share package formats and tools:

  • Debian family: Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, Raspberry Pi OS. Packages are .deb, managed with apt/dpkg.
  • Red Hat family: RHEL, Fedora, CentOS Stream, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux. Packages are .rpm, managed with dnf/rpm.
  • SUSE: openSUSE and SUSE Linux Enterprise, with zypper and RPM.

Enterprise distributions (RHEL, SLES, Ubuntu LTS with Pro) offer long life cycles and paid support. LTS means long-term support. Rolling releases (Arch, openSUSE Tumbleweed) update continuously instead of in versions.

Know examples by category: office (LibreOffice), web browsing (Firefox, Chromium), email (Thunderbird), graphics (GIMP, Inkscape), 3D (Blender), media (VLC). On servers: web (Apache httpd, NGINX), databases (MariaDB, PostgreSQL), file sharing (Samba for SMB, NFS), mail (Postfix), remote access (OpenSSH). Programming languages common on Linux include C, Python, Bash, Perl, and JavaScript. Desktop environments such as GNOME, KDE Plasma, and Xfce run on a display server (Wayland or X11).

guide.h: Licenses and the open source model
guide.html:
Free software (FSF) is about freedom: to run, study, change, and share. Open source (OSI) is a closely related definition with a focus on development benefits. Licenses split into two groups:

  • Copyleft (GPL, AGPL, LGPL): if you distribute a modified version, it must stay under the same license with source code.
  • Permissive (MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0): you can include the code in closed-source products, keeping the copyright notice.

Companies earn money from open source with support subscriptions, services, training, hosting, and open-core add-ons. Creative Commons licenses cover content such as documentation and images.

guide.h: Where Linux runs, and staying safe
guide.html: Linux runs on physical machines, virtual machines (a full guest OS on a hypervisor), containers (isolated processes sharing the host kernel, run with Podman or Docker), cloud instances launched from images and configured with cloud-init, and on Windows through WSL. Version 2.0 also expects everyday security sense: unique long passwords in a password manager, MFA and passkeys where possible, encrypted connections (HTTPS, SSH), and keeping software updated.

tips: Ubuntu and Mint are Debian-based (.deb, apt); Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, and Alma are Red Hat-based (.rpm, dnf).
GPL = copyleft; MIT, BSD, Apache = permissive.
Samba = Windows file sharing; Apache/NGINX = web; MariaDB = database; Postfix = mail.
Containers share the host kernel; VMs run their own kernel.
"Free" in free software means freedom, not price.
terms: The core of the OS that manages hardware, memory, and processes.
A complete OS built around the Linux kernel.
Long-term support release with extended updates.
License rule that derivatives must keep the same license.
License allowing reuse in closed-source software (MIT, BSD, Apache).
Isolated processes sharing the host kernel, with their own filesystem image.
Tool that configures cloud instances at first boot.
Windows Subsystem for Linux: run Linux tools on Windows.

slides.title: Linux and open source
script: Welcome to the first Linux Essentials module. Here you'll learn what Linux actually is, how distributions differ, and how open source licensing works.
This topic is vocabulary-heavy, so focus on recognizing names and categories.

slides.title: Distribution families
script: Linux by itself is a kernel. A distribution adds tools, a package manager, and applications.
Debian, Ubuntu, and Mint use deb packages and apt. RHEL, Fedora, Rocky, and AlmaLinux use RPM and dnf. SUSE uses RPM with zypper.

slides.title: Open source applications
script: Know common open source applications by category. LibreOffice is the office suite, Firefox the browser, GIMP and Inkscape edit images.
On servers, Apache and NGINX serve web pages, MariaDB and PostgreSQL store data, Samba shares files with Windows, and OpenSSH provides secure remote access.

slides.title: Open source licenses
script: Free software means the freedom to run, study, change, and share a program. It isn't about price.
Copyleft licenses like the GPL require modified versions to stay open when distributed. Permissive licenses like MIT and Apache let companies reuse code in closed products.

slides.title: Where Linux runs
script: Linux runs almost everywhere: on servers, desktops, phones, and embedded devices.
Virtual machines run a full guest kernel, containers share the host's kernel, cloud instances start from images configured by cloud-init, and WSL brings Linux tools to Windows.

slides.title: Review: Linux and open source
script: You've finished the Linux and open source module. Go back over the key terms and try each command in a terminal or in the labs.
Then take the Linux and open source question set and read every explanation. Then try the labs for hands-on practice.

modules.title: Command line basics
modules.summary: Use the Bash shell confidently: command syntax, variables and quoting, history and completion, getting help from man pages, and navigating and managing files and directories.

guide.html: Topic 012 is 9 of 40 points: command-line usage, documentation, paths, and file management. Expect to recognize the right command and option, and to fill in a command from memory.

A command has the form command -options arguments. The shell (usually Bash) expands variables and wildcards before running it. Variables: NAME=value (no spaces) creates a shell variable, export NAME makes it visible to programs, and $NAME reads it. PATH lists the directories searched for commands; HOME is your home directory. Quotes matter: double quotes expand $VAR, single quotes keep text literal, and a backslash escapes one character.

Time savers: Tab completes names, history lists past commands, !! repeats the last one, and Ctrl+R searches history.

man command opens the manual page; man 5 passwd picks section 5 (file formats) instead of section 1 (commands). Section 8 is administration commands. man -k word or apropos word searches descriptions. command --help prints a summary, info opens GNU info pages, and help covers Bash builtins such as cd. which and type show where a command comes from.

Paths starting with / are absolute; others are relative to the working directory. . is the current directory, .. the parent, ~ your home. Key directories (FHS): /etc config, /home users, /var logs and changing data, /tmp temporary files, /usr installed software, /boot kernel, /dev devices, /proc and /sys kernel information. Hidden files start with a dot.

ls -la lists everything in detail. cd, pwd, mkdir -p, touch, cp -r, mv, rm, rm -r, rmdir. Wildcards: * any characters, ? one character, [a-c] one from a set. Links: ln file hardlink creates another name for the same inode; ln -s target link creates a pointer that breaks if the target is removed. find dir -name 'pattern' searches in real time; locate uses a database. file identifies content type.

tips: No spaces around = when assigning variables.
Double quotes expand variables; single quotes don't.
man 1 = commands, man 5 = file formats, man 8 = admin commands.
cp needs -r for directories; rmdir only removes empty directories.
* matches many characters, ? exactly one.
terms: A path from the root, starting with /.
A path from the current directory.
Directories the shell searches for commands.
Makes a variable available to child processes.
Another directory entry for the same inode.
A file that points to another path.
Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: where files belong.

slides.title: Command line basics
script: This module covers the Bash shell: how commands are built, how to get help, and how to move around and manage files.
Type along in a terminal or the labs as you go.

slides.title: Anatomy of a command
script: Every command follows the same pattern: the command name, then options that change its behavior, then arguments it acts on.
Variables hold values, and quoting controls expansion: double quotes expand variables, single quotes keep text literal.

slides.title: Getting help
script: When you don't remember an option, the manual pages are always installed. man ls shows the ls manual.
Sections matter: section 1 is commands, 5 is configuration file formats, and 8 is administration commands. apropos finds commands by keyword.

slides.title: The Linux directory tree
script: Linux uses a single tree starting at the root, slash. The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard says where things go.
Configuration lives in etc, logs in var log, users' files in home, temporary files in tmp, and installed programs under usr.

slides.title: Managing files
script: Create directories with mkdir dash p, copy with cp dash r for directories, move or rename with mv, and remove with rm.
Wildcards let one command act on many files. Links give a file another name: hard links share the inode, symbolic links point to a path.

slides.title: Review: command line basics
script: You've finished the command line basics module. Go back over the key terms and try each command in a terminal or in the labs.
Then take the command line basics question set and read every explanation. Then try the labs for hands-on practice.

modules.title: The power of the command line: data processing
modules.summary: Archive and compress files, redirect input and output, chain commands with pipes, search and transform text with grep, sed, cut, sort, and uniq, and write simple Bash scripts with variables, tests, and loops.

guide.html: Topic 013 is 9 of 40 points: archives and compression, redirection and text processing, and basic shell scripting (the biggest single objective at 4 points).

tar bundles files; compression is separate. tar -czf out.tar.gz dir creates a gzip archive, -j uses bzip2, -J uses xz. tar -tf lists and tar -xf extracts (add -C dir to choose where). Single-file tools: gzip/gunzip, bzip2/bunzip2, xz/unxz. zip/unzip handle .zip files. xz compresses smallest but slowest; gzip is fastest.

Every program has stdin (0), stdout (1), and stderr (2). > writes output to a file (overwrite), >> appends, < reads input from a file, 2> redirects errors, and 2>/dev/null discards them. A pipe | feeds one command's output into the next: grep sshd /var/log/auth.log | wc -l. tee writes to a file and the screen at once.

grep finds lines (-i ignore case, -v invert, -c count, -r recursive). head/tail show the start or end (tail -f follows logs), less pages, wc -l counts lines, sort (-n numeric, -r reverse), uniq -c counts adjacent duplicates (so sort first), cut -d: -f1 takes fields, sed 's/old/new/g' replaces text, and diff compares files. Regex basics: ^ start of line, $ end, . any character, * repeat, [0-9] a set.

A script starts with a shebang such as #!/bin/bash and needs execute permission (chmod +x). Arguments arrive as $1, $2...; $# is the count, $0 the script name, $? the last exit status (0 = success). Use $(command) to capture output. Conditions use if [ -f file ]; then ... fi, with tests such as -f (file exists), -d (directory), = (strings equal), and -eq (numbers equal). Loops: for f in *.log; do ...; done and while. End with exit 0 or a non-zero code on failure.

tips: tar: c create, x extract, t list, f file; z/j/J = gzip/bzip2/xz.
> overwrites, >> appends, 2> errors.
Sort before uniq, or duplicates that aren't adjacent stay separate.
$# counts arguments; $1 is the first; $? is the last exit status.
[ -f ] tests files, [ -d ] directories; -eq compares numbers, = compares strings.
terms: Standard output (1) and standard error (2) streams.
| connects one command's output to another's input.
A pattern that matches text, such as ^error.
Number a command returns; 0 means success.
Tool that bundles files into one archive.
Removes or counts adjacent duplicate lines.

slides.title: Processing data
script: This module is about the real power of the command line: combining small tools to search, count, transform, and archive data, and then saving those steps as scripts.
Practice each command; the exam often asks you to complete one.

slides.title: Archives and compression
bullets: c x t f z j J
script: tar bundles many files into one archive. Compression is a separate step that tar can call with z for gzip, j for bzip2, or capital J for xz.
Create with c, extract with x, list with t, and always give the file name with f.

slides.title: Redirection and pipes
script: Programs read standard input and write standard output and standard error. You can send any of these to files.
A pipe sends one command's output into the next, so small tools combine into powerful one-liners.

slides.title: Text tools
script: grep finds lines, sort orders them, uniq counts duplicates, and wc counts lines. cut pulls out fields and sed replaces text.
Regular expressions describe patterns: caret for the start of a line, dollar for the end, dot for any character, and brackets for sets.

slides.title: Your first script
script: A script is a text file of commands. Start it with a shebang so the system knows to use bash, and make it executable with chmod plus x.
Scripts read arguments as dollar one, dollar two, and so on, test conditions with if and square brackets, repeat work with for loops, and report success with an exit status of zero.

slides.title: Review: data processing
script: You've finished the data processing module. Go back over the key terms and try each command in a terminal or in the labs.
Then take the data processing question set and read every explanation. Then try the labs for hands-on practice.

modules.title: The Linux operating system: administration basics
modules.summary: Understand installation and provisioning, hardware and device files, the boot process, processes and services with systemd, system logs, package management, and basic network configuration and troubleshooting with iproute2 tools.

guide.html: Topic 014 is 8 of 40 points: installation and provisioning, hardware and device access, processes and logs (3 points), and network configuration.

Physical and virtual machines install from an ISO; cloud instances start from images configured by cloud-init. The boot process: firmware (UEFI/BIOS) → bootloader (GRUB) → kernel and initramfs → systemd (PID 1) → services and login. Hardware: lsblk (disks), lscpu, lspci, lsusb, free -h (memory), df -h (disk space), dmesg (kernel messages). Devices appear as files in /dev (/dev/sda, /dev/nvme0n1); /proc and /sys expose kernel information.

ps aux lists processes; top shows them live. kill PID sends SIGTERM (polite stop); kill -9 forces it. systemctl status|start|stop|restart|enable|disable name manages services; enable means start at boot. Logs: journalctl reads the systemd journal (-u sshd for one service, -f to follow, -b this boot); text logs live in /var/log. dmesg shows kernel messages. Packages install from signed repositories: apt install on Debian/Ubuntu, dnf install on Fedora/RHEL.

Version 2.0 uses iproute2: ip addr (addresses), ip route (routes and default gateway), ss -tlnp (listening ports). Older equivalents are ifconfig, route, and netstat. DNS servers are listed in /etc/resolv.conf; static names in /etc/hosts. Test with ping, dig or host (DNS), and traceroute/tracepath. Know private address ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) and that IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.

tips: Boot: firmware → GRUB → kernel → systemd (PID 1).
systemctl enable = start at boot; start = start now.
journalctl -u name shows one service's logs.
ip addr, ip route, ss replace ifconfig, route, netstat.
/etc/resolv.conf = DNS servers; /etc/hosts = static names.
terms: A running program with a PID.
Message to a process, such as SIGTERM or SIGKILL.
systemd's log store, read with journalctl.
Installs, updates, and removes software from repositories.
Router used for destinations outside the local network.

slides.title: System administration basics
script: This module introduces the system side of Linux: how it boots, how to see hardware and processes, where logs are, and how networking is configured.
These are the first skills of a junior administrator.

slides.title: How Linux boots
script: When you power on, the firmware runs first, then the GRUB bootloader loads the kernel and an initial RAM disk.
The kernel starts systemd as process 1, which brings up services and the login screen.

slides.title: Processes and services
script: ps aux lists every process and top shows them live. kill asks a process to stop, and kill dash nine forces it.
systemctl controls services: start and stop now, enable and disable at boot. journalctl reads their logs.

slides.title: Hardware and software
script: Hardware tools show disks, CPUs, memory, and free space. Devices are files under dev, and the kernel exposes information under proc and sys.
Install software from repositories with apt on Debian and Ubuntu, or dnf on Fedora and Red Hat.

slides.title: Networking with iproute2
script: Use ip addr to see addresses, ip route to see the default gateway, and ss to see listening ports.
DNS servers are in resolv.conf, static names in etc hosts. Test with ping, dig, and traceroute.

slides.title: Review: system administration basics
script: You've finished the system administration basics module. Go back over the key terms and try each command in a terminal or in the labs.
Then take the system administration basics question set and read every explanation. Then try the labs for hands-on practice.

modules.title: Security and file system permissions
modules.summary: Manage users and groups, read and set permissions and ownership, understand special bits and special directories, use sudo responsibly, and log in and transfer files securely with SSH and keys.

guide.html: Topic 015 is 7 of 40 points: remote logins and elevated privileges, users and groups, permissions and ownership, and special files and directories.

Accounts live in /etc/passwd (name, UID, GID, home, shell); password hashes in /etc/shadow (root-only); groups in /etc/group. root is UID 0; regular users usually start at 1000; system accounts run services. Commands: useradd -m, passwd, usermod -aG group user (append), userdel, groupadd, id, who, last. Use sudo for single admin commands (logged, no shared password); su - switches user with that user's password.

ls -l shows -rwxr-x---: type, then owner, group, and others. r=4, w=2, x=1, so rwxr-x--- is 750. chmod 640 file or chmod u+x,o-r file changes modes; chown user:group file changes ownership (root only); chgrp changes just the group. On directories, r lists names, w creates and deletes entries, and x lets you enter. Special bits: SUID (runs as the file's owner, like passwd), SGID (on directories, new files inherit the group), and the sticky bit (only owners can delete their files, like /tmp). umask sets default permissions for new files.

Use SSH (ssh user@host) instead of Telnet, and scp/sftp instead of FTP. Key-based login: ssh-keygen creates a key pair; ssh-copy-id user@host installs the public key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Keep the private key private, ideally with a passphrase. Special directories: /tmp and /var/tmp are world-writable with the sticky bit.

tips: usermod -aG adds a group; without -a it replaces groups.
/etc/shadow holds password hashes and is root-only.
SUID = run as owner; SGID dir = inherit group; sticky = only owner deletes.
ssh-copy-id installs your public key; never share the private key.
terms: File with password hashes and aging, readable only by root.
Special bit: program runs with its owner's privileges.
Directory bit: only a file's owner can delete it.
Runs one command with elevated rights, with logging.
Server file listing public keys allowed to log in.

slides.title: Security and permissions
script: The final module covers who can do what on a Linux system: accounts, groups, file permissions, and secure remote access.
Permissions questions often give you an ls line or an octal number, so practice converting between them.

slides.title: Users and groups
script: Account details are in etc passwd, password hashes in etc shadow, and groups in etc group. Root is user zero.
Create users with useradd dash m, add them to groups with usermod dash a capital G, and use sudo for administrative commands.

slides.title: Reading permissions
script: Each file has permissions for its owner, its group, and everyone else. Read is four, write is two, execute is one.
So rwx r-x r-x is 755. On directories, execute means you can enter, and write means you can create or delete files inside.

slides.title: Special bits
script: Three special bits change behavior. SUID makes a program run with its owner's rights, which is how passwd updates the shadow file.
SGID on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group, and the sticky bit on tmp stops users from deleting each other's files.

slides.title: Secure remote access
script: SSH encrypts remote logins and file transfers. Use scp or sftp to copy files.
For key-based logins, generate a key pair with ssh-keygen and copy the public key to the server with ssh-copy-id. The private key never leaves your computer.

slides.title: Review: security and permissions
script: You've finished the security and permissions module. Go back over the key terms and try each command in a terminal or in the labs.
Then take the security and permissions question set and read every explanation. Then try the labs for hands-on practice.
